aic:36654.summary: Two faces of a small gold coin are shown side by side: on one, the emperor Basil I and his son Constantine hold a long patriarchal cross between them; on the other, Christ sits frontally on a throne, haloed, blessing and holding the Gospel book, encircled by the Latin legend naming him King of kings. After more than a century of debate over sacred images, the return of Christ to the gold coinage declared the triumph of the icon in the everyday currency of the empire.
facts: The Art Institute of Chicago records the inscription IhS XPS REX REGNANTIUM ('Jesus Christ, King of those who reign') with the enthroned Christ, and bASILIOS ET CONSTANTI AUGG with the imperial pair.
The museum notes that Basil I's coin, with Christ enthroned on its front, was a radical departure from the coinage of the iconoclast emperors, after the Iconoclastic Controversy of about 730–843.
The coin is about 2 cm in diameter and was a gift of Emily Crane Chadbourne (accession 1940.23).
aic:36654.notes: AIC dates it 868–870; Basil I reigned 867–886. Which face is technically obverse follows the museum (Christ on the front).
